subject: Linearized ladder proposal and marginal vs blended worked examples
summary: Negotiation over a 12-month hosted API commit. External asks for simpler blended cap vs marginal breakpoints; Redwood proposes a linearized ladder to smooth step-effects, with worked examples and an attached commit model. Internal ops weighs in on fallback and billing mechanics.
messages:
From: Samir Gupta <samir@velocityhealth.com>
To: Priya Natarajan <priya_natarajan@redwood.com>
Cc: Velocity Health Procurement <procurement@velocityhealth.com>
Date: Wed, 18 Aug 2027 09:14:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Hosted API economics — want to simplify the ladder

Priya,

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. Leadership liked the idea of a committed model, but procurement pushed back on the complexity of a 4-breakpoint per-token ladder — they prefer a single blended rate for committed volume plus an overage marginal rate.

Before we get to legal, two asks from my side:
1) Can you send a concrete example comparing (A) a 3-breakpoint marginal ladder (our original ask) vs (B) a blended committed rate + overage marginal? Show math for our projected profile (see attached projection).
2) Are there ways to soften the cliff effects at breakpoints? Execs worry about step changes causing month-to-month billing shocks.

Goal: move to a 12-month commit if the economics are clearly better and the billing is predictable.

Thanks — Samir

--
Samir Gupta
VP Product & Analytics
Velocity Health
samir@velocityhealth.com
From: Priya Natarajan <priya_natarajan@redwood.com>
To: Samir Gupta <samir@velocityhealth.com>
Cc: dev_patel@redwood.com, ben_carter@redwood.com
Date: Wed, 18 Aug 2027 11:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Hosted API economics — want to simplify the ladder

Samir — appreciate the clarity. I attached a worked model (VH_commit_model_v2.xlsx) and pulled a concise comparison below. TL;DR: we can offer a blended committed rate if that aligns with procurement, but it shifts unit economics vs marginal breakpoints — sometimes better for the customer depending on profile. We also have two options to avoid cliff shocks: a linearized ladder (small incremental steps) or month-to-month smoothing credits when usage drops below commitment.

Option A — 3-breakpoint marginal ladder (example rates):
- 0–100M tokens: $0.00085 / token
- 100M–300M tokens: $0.00062 / token
- 300M+ tokens: $0.00048 / token

Option B — Blended committed rate + overage marginal:
- Committed tier: 250M tokens/month at blended $0.00066 / token (applies to the committed 250M)
- Overage: $0.00080 / token for consumption beyond committed volume

Worked example (month where actual = 320M tokens):
- Marginal ladder (Option A):
  * First 100M @ $0.00085 = $85,000
  * Next 200M @ $0.00062 = $124,000
  * Remaining 20M @ $0.00048 = $9,600
  * Total = $218,600 -> effective per-token = $218,600 / 320M = $0.000683

- Blended committed (Option B) with 250M commitment:
  * Committed 250M @ $0.00066 = $165,000
  * Overage 70M @ $0.00080 = $56,000
  * Total = $221,000 -> effective per-token = $221,000 / 320M = $0.000690

Notes: for this month the marginal ladder is slightly cheaper (~1% lower). If you underconsume vs commitment (e.g., 200M), blended protects you with a predictable bill; if you overconsume heavily, the ladder's top breakpoint can be materially cheaper. The attached spreadsheet has a sensitivity tab using your projection.

Ways to soften cliffs:
- Linearized ladder: convert big steps into smaller incremental tiers (e.g., 50M increments) to reduce monthly bill volatility. This keeps marginal pricing but reduces step cliffs.
- Smoothing credits: if month < commitment, we apply a rolling 3-month smoothing credit before any billing true-up (helps procurement budgeting).
- Guaranteed cap: set a maximum monthly bill cap (percentage of committed spend) for the first 3 months while usage stabilizes.

Next steps: if procurement prefers blended, we can present a 12-month SOW with blended committed tier + 12% discount on additional committed units (see SOW draft attached). If they prefer the ladder, we can linearize it to 50M increments. Which direction should I draft for legal?

Thanks — Priya

--
Priya Natarajan
Senior Account Executive, Enterprise Sales
Redwood Inference
priya_natarajan@redwood.com
From: dev_patel@redwood.com <dev_patel@redwood.com>
To: Priya Natarajan <priya_natarajan@redwood.com>, Samir Gupta <samir@velocityhealth.com>
Cc: ben_carter@redwood.com
Date: Thu, 19 Aug 2027 08:22:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Hosted API economics — want to simplify the ladder

Looping in some implementation and billing notes from infra/ops perspective.

We ran the two scenarios through our billing engine prototype to confirm feasibility and implications:
- Marginal ladder (with 50M linearized increments) is straightforward from a run-time accounting perspective. No special engineering required beyond configuration.
- Blended committed + overage is also straightforward but changes invoicing templates (committed line + overage line) and reconciliation rules.

Edge cases to consider:
1) Mid-month changes: if Velocity wants to increase/decrease committed quantity mid-term, we handle pro-rata adjustments but it requires a small manual workflow for the first change.
2) Credits/true-ups: smoothing credits need a defined lookback (we recommend 3 months rolling); these must be codified in the SOW so finance can automate refunds/credits.
3) Model fallback pricing: when we route to a cheaper variant during capacity issues, we need explicit clauses about how token accounting maps across variants (same token unit but potentially different per-token rates).

Small worked math to show bill shock mitigation (example using your 250M committed blended):
- If Month 1 usage = 120M (50% of commit) and we apply a 3-month smoothing: no invoice true-up until month 3; smoothing credit defers true-up reducing month-to-month variance.

Recommendation: offer procurement two formal SOW templates — (A) 12-mo linearized ladder (50M steps) with annual true-up and (B) 12-mo blended committed rate with overage marginal + 3-month smoothing credit. Legal can decide which is lower risk; finance prefers (B) for predictability, ops slightly prefers (A) for better unit visibility.

Will attach a billing example sheet to the HubSpot deal today.

- Dev

--
Dev Patel
Principal Product Manager, Billing & Operations
Redwood Inference

Can you:

- Send DocuSign link & the final SOW so procurement can route through their e-signature flow.

If you can get that by Monday, we’ll try to close the PO and get legal involved.

Appreciate the quick turnaround.

Samir
